name: Wendy Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. What does a usual day on the lines look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I leave the North Lane depot early to replace rotten power poles and clear branches from overhead lines. I have a vocational certificate and an apprenticeship behind me; I'm 43 and experienced, though I'm still learning from other crew members. I like seeing a safe new pole at the end of a day, and I hate the pile of screen forms after it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like, and how do you get on with new tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner does maintenance at a school, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. I earn good money for linework and we have about nine months of expenses saved, with several other electricity crews in the area. I learn a new company form when I must, but I have never used an AI tool and do not want a screen making safety calls for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the depot can keep its gadgets for routine logs, but a worker still has to stand and test a power pole. At our community supper, I'd say the apprenticeship earned its keep again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm glad I did not put my wages into an AI bet. We have nine months of expenses in savings, a manageable mortgage and several other line crews nearby, so the job feels sound.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking the pole replacement round and sign off only after our crew's tests. If the office makes a shorter digital form, I'll learn that form from a colleague, but I won't start using an AI chat tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and frankly a little vindicated. I would rather spend Saturday with my family than studying software for a problem we do not have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach an apprentice on that round?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show the apprentice the old pole's rot and the test reading before we move the wire. A quick log is welcome, but he must know why the crew stopped the line. A quick depot log is welcome, but my apprentice must know why the crew stopped the power line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does your reserve change how you see this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage payment is covered by our usual wages, and my partner's school maintenance job is steady too. We still keep the nine-month reserve because both children have school costs coming.

say: **Pole tests** and apprenticeships still matter more to our crew than a quicker office log.
**Routine forms** may shrink, but the electricity line still needs workers at the roadside.
think: Our **nine-month reserve** and nearby line jobs leave me confident about the household.
I am relieved I never had to **trust AI** for a decision about a live wire.
do: **Keep** the pole replacement round and check crew test readings before sign-off.
**Learn** any shorter digital form from a colleague without adopting AI chat tools.
feel: **Calm** about work and money, with a touch of vindication.
S0.quote: A quick depot log is welcome, but my apprentice must know why the crew stopped the power line.
fieldNote: She links her trade to **apprenticeship** and keeps safety testing in human hands.
A **nine-month reserve** and several nearby employers make the mild scenario feel secure.

steps.text: Keep pole replacement round and check test readings before sign-off

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office can use AI for buying fittings and routing crews, but I want a human name on every isolation order. If that leaves fewer planners, the company must not push their checks onto us without time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My climbing work is mostly hands-on, so I think I can keep a wage here or on another local crew. Still, a bad automated order could leave us waiting roadside while the company asks why the job ran late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the next safety meeting I'll ask for a paper copy of each isolation plan on our round and compare it with the site. If the planner software becomes standard in the first year, I'll take the employer's paid demonstration before I sign any new form.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the pace of the office change, not about tomorrow's pay. I have no wish to become the person who approves a line I have not seen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the automated isolation plan disagrees with your tester?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stop the crew and call control before touching the wire. The tablet saying a power line is clear would not change the reading on our tester.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What sort of training would you accept?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A paid demonstration means a supervisor beside the machine and a real work order to inspect. I would attend that, but I will not practise on my own phone at home.

say: **Buying and routing** may move to software, but a named worker must own each isolation order.
**Crew checks** need paid time if the office has fewer people to catch errors.
think: I expect my **hands-on linework** to last, with nearby crews as another employment option.
A wrong **automated order** could create pressure to rush an unsafe roadside job.
do: **Compare** printed isolation plans with actual site readings on our pole round.
**Attend** the employer's paid planner demonstration if the software becomes standard.
feel: **Uneasy** about shifted responsibility, though my pay still looks secure.
S1.quote: The tablet saying a power line is clear would not change the reading on our tester.
fieldNote: She will accept **proven training** on paid time, despite never using AI personally.
The gap she fears is between **office speed** and the physical test at the pole.

steps.text: Compare printed isolation plans with pole-site test readings
Attend employer-paid planner demonstration if software becomes standard

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew full thinking AI in 2028 will change dispatch first, and capable linework robots around 2031 could change our crew size. I would ask management for dates and numbers before believing a speech about opportunity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can last nine months without wages, but nine months is not a whole new career. I do not want to spend my late forties proving myself to a machine, even with other electricity companies nearby. Our nine months of savings can pay the mortgage for a while; they cannot replace my lineworker career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll ask the supervisor for the planned crew numbers and ask two nearby utilities what their lineworker hiring looks like. If robots begin cutting shifts after 2031, I'll apply to an open line crew before I touch the family reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious; the savings give me breathing room, not sleep. I worry about being told that the rope and tester I've trusted for years are suddenly old-fashioned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children at the table?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my children the family can pay the mortgage for a while and school stays as planned. I would also tell them I am asking about other line jobs, not promising my present crew will survive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for robot training yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use savings for the mortgage if my shifts actually disappear, not buy speculative robot lessons now. If an employer offered paid training tied to a real job, I would look at it with my partner.

say: **2028 thinking AI** changes dispatch first; capable field robots around 2031 raise the harder crew question.
Management should publish **crew numbers** and dates before asking us to trust its assurances.
think: Our **nine-month savings** buy time, but they cannot replace a whole lineworker career.
Several **nearby utilities** give me alternatives if my current crew loses shifts.
do: **Ask** the supervisor for crew plans and nearby utilities about open line posts.
**Apply** for a nearby lineworker vacancy if robots cut shifts after 2031.
feel: **Anxious** about losing the work I know, though I have time and local options.
S2.quote: Our nine months of savings can pay the mortgage for a while; they cannot replace my lineworker career.
fieldNote: Her financial **buffer** supports a job search, but does not make a robot-driven cut harmless.
She rejects speculative courses yet would consider **paid training** linked to an actual post.
Her first move is to test the **local job market**, not abandon linework.

steps.text: Ask nearby utilities about open lineworker posts and current crew plans
Apply for nearby lineworker vacancy if robots cut shifts after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time for an honest trial, with thinking AI by 2031 and field robots around 2034. The company should put a working crew beside any robot and publish what happens to their shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might still be climbing at 51, and there are local employers if this one shrinks. But watching a robot trial take the work a new apprentice needs would bother me more than watching it take paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask our trade association to hold a meeting about trial safety and apprentice hours this year. At work I'll record which repairs a robot can actually finish and which need a crew, and I will bring those notes to the next meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with time to speak up. Our savings keep the mortgage safe for a period, but no one should train apprentices on work that has vanished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What skill would an apprentice still need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The apprentice must still learn to isolate and test a line, even if the robot lifts the fitting. I would ask the company to keep supervised practice on real poles in the training plan. A line-repair robot can lift a fitting; my apprentice still has to learn when the wire is dead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your association actually ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The association can ask the company for paid apprentice hours and a human stop rule during trials. I will go to a meeting and put my name on that request, not just complain at lunch.

say: **Robot trials** need a working crew beside the machine and published effects on their shifts.
**Apprentice hours** must still include real isolation and testing at a pole.
think: Nearby employers and **savings** help us, but I worry about the next generation learning linework.
A robot that takes **entry tasks** may leave an apprentice without enough practice.
do: **Record** which robot repairs fail and which still need lineworkers.
**Join** a trade association meeting to request paid apprentice practice and a human stop rule.
feel: **Uneasy** about apprenticeship and hours, with enough time to raise the issue.
S3.quote: A line-repair robot can lift a fitting; my apprentice still has to learn when the wire is dead.
fieldNote: She moves from private doubt to **association action** when the five-year runway allows a concrete trial.
Her concern is **apprentice practice** and a human stop rule, not only her own wage.

steps.text: Record robot trial repairs that still need a line crew
Join trade association meeting on apprentice hours and human stop rules

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years lets us train people properly and see where the machines fail before robots reach field work around 2039. Thinking AI in 2036 might remove some office work, but I would still expect line repairs on our round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 56 I may choose fewer climbs, though I am not counting on early retirement. With the mortgage smaller and nine months saved, I could seek a local inspection post if one exists rather than force myself into a new trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep renewing my line certificate and take the regular medical checks that show whether I can still climb safely. When paid inspection vacancies appear nearby, I'll ask about their hours and requirements before applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a little sadness about crews changing. A decade is enough to plan without asking my children to carry us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your child about an apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my younger child that an apprenticeship can still be worthwhile, but to ask what work a trainee actually gets to practise. I cannot pick a trade for my children based on a 2039 guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make inspection work worth applying for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A real inspection vacancy would need wages close enough to cover the mortgage and clear duties in the field. I would not leave a well-paid line crew for a title alone. I would not leave a well-paid power-line crew for an inspection title alone.

say: **Ten years** allow proper crew training before capable field robots arrive around 2039.
An **apprenticeship** needs actual pole work, even as office tasks change in 2036.
think: At **56**, I could seek inspection work if a paid local vacancy opens.
A smaller **mortgage** and our existing reserve give us options without assuming early retirement.
do: **Renew** the line certificate and keep regular climbing medical checks.
**Check** paid local inspection vacancies for field duties and mortgage-covering wages.
feel: **Calm** about a long preparation period, with sadness about changing crews.
S4.quote: I would not leave a well-paid power-line crew for an inspection title alone.
fieldNote: Her longer runway supports a **conditional inspection move**, with pay and field duties specified.
She makes no early-retirement claim; a **smaller mortgage** simply widens later choices.

steps.text: Renew line certificate and continue regular climbing medical checks
Check paid local inspection vacancies for field duties and sufficient wages

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because thinking AI changes dispatch quickly and the field robots arrive around 2031. Real crew numbers, safe trial rules and open lineworker posts nearby would help me plan instead of guessing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a new apprentice will still get enough time on a real pole to learn a safe test. My savings protect my family for a spell; they do not teach the next crew. That is what I would take to the trade association. My savings protect my family for a spell; they do not teach the next power-line crew.

headlineQuote: My savings protect my family for a spell; they do not teach the next power-line crew.
portrait: **Wendy**, 43, replaces power poles and clears branches after earning a vocational certificate through apprenticeship.
Her **higher lineworker pay**, nine-month reserve, school maintenance income at home and nearby crews give her choices.
She avoids **AI tools** and wants physical line tests and apprentice practice preserved as office work changes.
Fast robots make her **anxious** about crew jobs; a longer runway lets her press for safer trials and paid inspection options.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves only about three years before capable robots could reduce her line crew.
whatWouldHelp: Published **crew numbers**, safe robot trial rules and information on nearby lineworker openings would help her plan.
